final_value: H2: Can you get a mortgage with 1099 income? || Answer (exact): Yes. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and FHA generally treat 1099 pay like self-employment income: about two years of history, your tax returns, and the income left after Schedule C expenses. If that supports the loan, the agency route usually costs less. If not, some non-QM lenders qualify you from the 1099s themselves, on terms that vary by lender. || Note: Add a next line: '1099 loans are one of several non-QM loan options when the agency route falls short.' Link it to the hub.

final_value: H2: Who is a 1099 income loan a good fit for? || Answer (exact): It fits people paid on Form 1099-NEC, 1099-MISC or 1099-K whose clients pay well but whose deductions shrink the income on their return, especially with a steady record of 1099 work or earlier work in the same field. If your returns already show enough income, start with a conventional or FHA loan instead. || Note: KEEP the H3s 'Who it fits' and 'Who it may not fit'.
decided_by_rule: P0: no conflict; team row stands

final_value: H2: How do lenders count 1099 income? || Answer (exact): On the agency route, the lender starts with net profit on your Schedule C, adds back non-cash items such as depreciation, and averages it, usually over two years. On a 1099-only loan, the lender starts with your 1099 totals and may subtract an expense factor it sets. That difference is why write-offs matter so much. || Note: Turn the bold lead-ins into H3s: 'The agency route: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and FHA' and 'The non-QM 1099 route'. KEEP the table.

And a later refinance depends on your file then, so the loan should make sense on its own. || Note: KEEP the bullets, including the Reg Z prepayment-penalty line.

final_value: H2: What is a HELOC? || Answer (exact): A HELOC is a revolving line of credit secured by your home. You draw what you need during a draw period, pay interest on what you have drawn, then repay the balance over a repayment period, usually at a variable rate. It sits behind your first mortgage instead of replacing it. || Note: Keep the existing second paragraph (Align places standalone HELOCs through multiple wholesale lenders) as the follow-on line. It does not suit everyday spending. || Note: KEEP H3s 'Who it fits' and 'Who it may not fit' and their bullets.

final_value: H2: How does a HELOC work? || Answer (exact): During the draw period you borrow up to your limit, repay, and borrow again; the CFPB's example draw period is 10 years. When it ends, borrowing stops and the balance is repaid on your agreement's schedule, often at a noticeably higher payment. Most lines carry a variable rate: a public index, such as the prime rate, plus the lender's margin. || Note: Delete the duplicate eyebrow 'How it works' above the H2. final_value: H2: What are the risks of a HELOC? || Answer (exact): The payment can rise when the index moves and again when the draw period ends. A lender can freeze or reduce the line if your home's value falls significantly or your finances change for the worse. Some fees continue after closing. And your home is the collateral, so missed payments can put it at risk. || Note: KEEP the five existing bullets.

A mortgage that secures a line owes no state or county transfer tax. And the county register of deeds records it for a flat fee, currently $30 per document.

That does not make it unfinanceable. Some lenders keep these loans on their own books, as portfolio or non-QM loans, and set their own terms based on why the project failed. || Note: Merge the FAQ 'What does non-warrantable mean?' here and remove it from the FAQ. final_value: H2: What makes a condo non-warrantable? || Answer (exact): A project is non-warrantable when it fails Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac project standards. Common reasons under Fannie Mae's rules include commercial space above 35%, one owner holding too many units, litigation about safety or structure, critical repairs, hotel-style operation, dues delinquency above 15% of units, reserves below 10% of the budget, or a new project under 50% presold. || Note: KEEP the cited list. Turn the bold lead-ins into H3s: 'What a lender reviews' and 'Where a portfolio lender comes in'.
decided_by_rule: P0: no conflict; team row stands

final_value: H2: Who is a non-warrantable condo loan a good fit for? || Answer (exact): It fits buyers in a project that failed agency review over a lawsuit, investor concentration, thin reserves or commercial space; owners of units in mixed-use buildings; owners refinancing after a project lost its status; and buyers who can bring more cash to closing. It fits poorly when you need the smallest down payment a program allows. || Note: KEEP the H3s.
decided_by_rule: P0: no conflict; team row stands

final_value: H2: Is it a bad idea to buy a non-warrantable condo? || Answer (exact): Not automatically, but go in clear-eyed. Financing usually needs more cash and costs more, fewer lenders compete for the loan, and the label can limit resale buyers and a future refinance until the problem is fixed. The cause matters most: a lawsuit or deferred repairs can reach owners later through special assessments. || Note: KEEP the bullets. ADD H3 'Will it be hard to sell later?': 'While the project stays non-warrantable, your buyers are mostly cash buyers and buyers using portfolio loans. A cash-out refinance fits when you would replace your first mortgage anyway, or when your current rate is higher than today's options. A home equity loan or HELOC fits when you want to keep your first-mortgage rate and borrow only the new money. Closing costs on a cash-out apply to the whole balance.

final_value: H3: Can I change my mind later? || Answer: Yes, but unwinding costs money. A HELOC or home equity loan can later be paid off or folded into a refinance, and a cash-out refinance can be refinanced again, each with new closing costs. Choosing the structure that fits the goal now is cheaper than paying twice, which is why the three questions come first.
